newsitem.title: USA: Kasparov seeks win against computer Deep Blue.
newsitem.headline: Kasparov seeks win against computer Deep Blue.

text.p: World chess champion Garry Kasparov opened the fifth game on Saturday of his re-match against the supercomputer Deep Blue searching for the win that would put him in control of the $1.1 million contest.
Playing with the white pieces and the advantage of the first move, Kasparov chose the same opening king's knight move he used when he won the first game of the match on last Saturday.

The Russian grandmaster, tied in the match at two points after one win each and two consecutive draws, tightly clasped his head in his hands as the game started in a small playing room in a Manhattan office complex.

He sought to control the board's central squares in a formation known as the King's Indian Attack, shuffling a bishop five times in the opening 10 moves as the massive IBM calculating machine tried to turn the position in its favour.

Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess that can examine hundreds of millions of possible moves per second. It made some unconventional opening moves with the black pieces without creating a major weakness for itself, expert observers said.

"Kasparov cannot make a blunder, he does not have the luxury of a mistake because the computer's technical ability will punish him immediately," grandmaster Yasser Seirawan of the United States said. "He is getting very tense as it comes down to the last two games of the match to decide the winner."

The sixth and final game of the match was scheduled for Sunday. The winner will collect $700,000 and the loser $400,000 from the competition, a re-match following the human's victory over a weaker version of the machine in Philadelphia in February 1996.
Kasparov has had two days since Wednesday's fourth game to recover psychologically and physically from three punishing games in which he resigned in a drawn position and then was held to two draws.

"I couldn't prepare normally, I played games three and four in a big crisis," Kasparov was quoted as saying in an interview on his Web site www.club-kasparov.com. "I know Deep Blue can be beaten unless I'm not in the right mental condition."

The event is part chess match and part research project to help build computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations for applications such as weather forecasting, air traffic control and molecular dynamics, according to IBM.
The company said it had received millions of retrievals or "hits" on its Web site www.chess.ibm.com during the match and other Web sites have also reported great interest.
